key_insight: This paper shows that visual similarity is not one single score: people judge images differently depending on the aspect they care about, such as shape, color, texture, or semantics. The authors introduce a text-prompted perceptual metric that can adapt similarity judgments to the user’s intended criterion.
problem_solved: Existing image similarity metrics compress rich human judgments into one scalar value, which cannot express context-specific notions of similarity. This paper addresses the need for a metric that can evaluate images along multiple free-form semantic aspects instead of only a generic notion of closeness.
method: Collected a large-scale dataset of human similarity judgments on image triplets with annotations across multiple free-form semantic aspects.
Designed a text-prompted image perceptual metric that conditions similarity scoring on a natural-language description of the desired aspect.
Benchmarked the approach against existing perceptual metrics to evaluate whether it better matches human judgments across different similarity criteria.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more faithful evaluation of generative models, retrieval systems, and editing tools when the notion of similarity depends on the task. It also provides a more flexible way to compare images in applications where color, shape, style, or meaning may matter differently.

paper_title: The Many Senses of Visual Similarity: A Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Metric
paper_authors: Sheng-Yu Wang, Yotam Nitzan, Aaron Hertzmann, Jun-Yan Zhu, Eli Shechtman
